note: Hand-authored editorial seed for the margin rail and tap-to-define. `glossary` is the work-level annotation dictionary (CONTENT_PIPELINE/BIBLE §8.1): curated in-context entries with aliases so a tap resolves across editions (Butler/Pope use Roman names + patronymics). Chapter overviews are keyed by book number; passages carry people/connections keyed by edition-specific sectionId. The pipeline does not overwrite this file.

chapters.1: A plague tears through the Greek camp, and a furious quarrel erupts between Agamemnon and Achilles over a captive woman. Achilles withdraws from the war and begs his goddess mother to make the Greeks pay for the insult.
chapters.2: Agamemnon, tricked by a false dream, tests his weary army by proposing they sail home, and nearly loses them when they bolt for the ships. Order is restored, and the great armies on both sides muster for battle.
chapters.3: Paris, who started the war by stealing Helen, challenges her husband Menelaus to single combat to settle everything. From the walls of Troy, Helen and old King Priam watch the duel unfold.
chapters.4: A broken truce reignites the war when an arrow strikes Menelaus. Agamemnon rouses his captains up and down the lines, and the two armies crash together in the day's first great slaughter.
chapters.5: Diomedes goes on a god-touched rampage, cutting down Trojans and even wounding the gods Aphrodite and Ares on the field. It is one warrior's furious finest hour.
chapters.6: Amid the fighting, two enemies discover an old family bond and part as friends instead of foes. Inside the walls, Hector shares a tender, aching farewell with his wife Andromache and their baby son.
chapters.7: Hector and the giant Ajax fight a long duel that ends only when night falls and they part with gifts of respect. The exhausted Greeks bury their dead and throw up a defensive wall around their ships.
chapters.8: Zeus forbids the other gods to meddle, then tips the scales toward Troy himself. By nightfall Hector has driven the Greeks back behind their wall, and the triumphant Trojans camp out on the open plain.
chapters.9: With the war turning against them, the Greek leaders send an embassy to Achilles, offering treasure and honors if he will return. Still nursing his wound, Achilles refuses them all.
chapters.10: Under cover of darkness, Odysseus and Diomedes slip out to spy on the Trojan camp. They catch an enemy scout, wring information from him, and carry out a deadly night raid.
chapters.11: Agamemnon storms through the battlefield until a wound forces him out, and one by one the Greek champions fall injured. Watching the chaos, Achilles sends his beloved friend Patroclus to find out how bad it has become.
chapters.12: The Trojans press hard against the Greek wall, and Hector leads the charge that finally breaks through it. The fighting reaches the very edge of the Greek ships.
chapters.13: With the sea god Poseidon secretly aiding the Greeks, the battle surges back and forth around the ships. Idomeneus stands out among the defenders holding the line.
chapters.14: Hera seduces and lulls Zeus to sleep so the gods can swing the fight back to the Greeks. Hector is wounded and the Trojans are driven into retreat, at least for a while.
chapters.15: Zeus wakes, furious, and turns the tide once more, sending the Greeks reeling back to their ships. The Trojans close in with fire, threatening to burn the fleet and end the war.
chapters.16: Unable to watch his comrades die, Patroclus borrows Achilles' armor and storms into battle, driving the Trojans back from the burning ships. His triumph carries him too far, to a fatal meeting with Hector.
chapters.17: A long, brutal struggle rages over the fallen body of Patroclus, as Greeks and Trojans fight to claim it. Neither side will yield the dead man to the other.
chapters.18: Achilles is shattered by grief and vows revenge, abandoning his quarrel at last. His mother visits the smith-god Hephaestus, who forges him a magnificent new suit of armor.
chapters.19: Achilles and Agamemnon are formally reconciled, the old feud set aside. Burning with rage and sorrow, Achilles puts on his new armor and returns to the war.
chapters.20: The gods take sides and join the fighting directly as Achilles tears into the Trojan ranks. Poseidon has to snatch the hero Aeneas to safety from Achilles' onslaught.
chapters.21: Achilles' slaughter so chokes the river Scamander with bodies that the river itself rises up to fight him. The gods clash among themselves while Achilles drives the panicked Trojans back through their gates.
chapters.22: Hector stands alone outside the walls to face Achilles while his parents beg him to come inside. Their final duel decides the fate that has loomed over Troy from the start.
chapters.23: Achilles holds a grand funeral for Patroclus, complete with athletic games where the Greek heroes compete in honor of the dead. It is a rare pause for mourning and ceremony amid the war.
chapters.24: Guided by the gods, old King Priam crosses into the enemy camp at night to beg Achilles for the body of his son Hector. The poem closes with grief, mercy, and Hector's funeral.

glossary.gloss: The greatest warrior among the Greeks — son of the mortal king Peleus and the sea-goddess Thetis, and leader of the Myrmidons. His rage is the engine of the whole poem: insulted by Agamemnon, he withdraws from the fighting and lets his own side suffer to make a point about honor.

Commander-in-chief of the Greek army and king of Mycenae — the most powerful of the Greek kings, and Menelaus' brother. Proud and quick to assert rank, he triggers the quarrel by seizing Achilles' prize.
King of Sparta and Agamemnon's brother. Helen was his wife; her flight to Troy with Paris is the cause of the war. The whole Greek expedition exists to win her back for him.

King of Ithaca, famous for cunning and persuasive speech. The Greeks' shrewdest tactician and diplomat — the one sent to argue, scheme, or smooth over a crisis. His own epic, the Odyssey, follows his long road home.

The aged king of Pylos and the army's elder statesman. Too old to fight at the front, he advises the younger kings, tells long stories of his youth, and tries to keep the peace between Achilles and Agamemnon.
The giant Greek warrior, son of Telamon — second only to Achilles in raw strength, the army's defensive wall. Steady and unshakable rather than clever. Carries a huge tower-like shield.
A second, smaller Ajax — son of Oïleus, swift on his feet, often fighting alongside the greater Ajax. Quick-tempered and less honorable than his namesake.
A young, fearless Greek king of Argos — in his great day on the battlefield he wounds even gods. One of the army's best fighters and most level-headed counselors.

Achilles' closest companion and dearest friend, gentle where Achilles is fierce. What happens to him is the hinge of the poem — it is grief over Patroclus that finally drives Achilles back into the war.
King of Crete and one of the older front-line Greek commanders, still a formidable spearman despite his years.
The army's chief prophet, who reads the will of the gods through birds and omens. It is his reading that exposes why Apollo sent the plague — and sets the quarrel in motion.
A captive woman awarded to Achilles as his prize of honor. When Agamemnon takes her to replace his own forfeited prize, the insult — not love — is what enrages Achilles.
The captive daughter of Chryses, a priest of Apollo, held by Agamemnon. His refusal to return her brings down Apollo's plague on the Greek camp.
A priest of Apollo and father of Chryseis. When Agamemnon insults him and refuses ransom for his daughter, he prays to Apollo, who answers with a plague.
An old warrior who helped raise Achilles and serves as a father-figure and tutor to him. Sent to plead with Achilles to return to battle.
The best archer among the Greeks and half-brother of the great Ajax, often sheltering behind Ajax's shield to loose his arrows.
Nestor's son — a brave, swift young Greek fighter and a close friend of Achilles.
A son of the healer Asclepius and the army's battlefield surgeon; when he is wounded the Greeks worry for the loss of his skill.
Achilles' loyal charioteer, who drives the immortal horses of his master into battle.

The greatest Trojan warrior and Troy's chief defender — eldest son of King Priam, husband of Andromache, father of the infant Astyanax. Brave and dutiful, he fights for his city and family rather than for glory. He is Achilles' great opponent.
The aged king of Troy, father of Hector, Paris, and many other sons. He watches the war devour his city and family from the walls, and his grief gives the poem its closing note.
A prince of Troy, son of Priam, whose abduction of Helen started the war. Handsome and a fine archer but reluctant in close combat — the Trojans often resent him for the ruin he brought.
The most beautiful woman in the world — wife of Menelaus, carried off to Troy by Paris. The war is fought over her. She lives among the Trojans full of regret and self-reproach.
Hector's devoted wife and mother of their infant son. Her farewell to Hector at the city wall is one of the poem's most tender and tragic scenes.
Queen of Troy, wife of Priam and mother of Hector and Paris. She pleads with her sons and mourns the city's losses.
A Trojan prince, son of Aphrodite, and one of Troy's strongest fighters after Hector. The gods protect him; tradition holds he will survive Troy's fall and found a new line.
A son of Zeus and leader of the Lycians, allies of Troy — one of the noblest warriors on the field. His reflections on why heroes must risk death state the poem's heroic code most clearly.
A Lycian captain and ally of Troy, companion of Sarpedon — remembered for exchanging armor and friendship with the Greek Diomedes on the battlefield.
A Trojan archer whose treacherous arrow shatters a sworn truce, reigniting the war.
A level-headed Trojan commander and Hector's advisor, who repeatedly counsels caution that Hector, to his cost, ignores.
A Trojan sent to spy on the Greek camp by night, caught and questioned in one of the poem's tensest episodes.
The infant son of Hector and Andromache — the small, vulnerable future of Troy, who famously cries at the sight of his father's helmet.
A wise elder of Troy who urges that Helen be returned to the Greeks to end the war.

King of the gods, lord of sky and thunder, who holds the ultimate balance of the war in his hands. He tries to honor a promise to Achilles' mother while keeping the other gods from tipping fate too far.
Queen of the gods, wife and sister of Zeus, and a fierce partisan of the Greeks. She schemes, argues, and even deceives Zeus to help the Greek side.
Goddess of wisdom, craft, and strategic war — Zeus's daughter and the Greeks' most powerful divine champion. She guides her favorites (Odysseus, Diomedes, Achilles) with cool intelligence.
God of archery, prophecy, healing, and plague — a leading supporter of the Trojans. He opens the poem by raining arrows of pestilence on the Greek camp.
God of the sea and earthquakes, brother of Zeus, and a backer of the Greeks. Powerful and resentful of Zeus's authority.
Goddess of love and beauty, mother of Aeneas, and a protector of Paris and the Trojans. Out of her element on the battlefield, where she is even wounded.
God of war in its raw, bloody, destructive form — fighting for the Trojans. Even the other gods find him hateful.
The lame smith-god of fire and craftsmanship, who forges armor for the gods and heroes — including a famous new shield for Achilles.
Goddess of the hunt and the wild, Apollo's twin sister, aligned with the Trojans.
The messenger god, guide and patron of travelers and cunning — who escorts Priam safely through the enemy camp.
A sea-goddess and the mother of Achilles. Devoted to her mortal son, she carries his appeals straight to Zeus and grieves the short life fate has given him.
The gods' swift messenger, who travels on the rainbow to carry their commands to mortals and to other gods.
God of the underworld and the realm of the dead itself — the shadowy place where the souls of slain heroes go.
A goddess, mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.
The river-god of Troy's great river, who rises in anger against Achilles when the slaughter chokes his waters.
One of Homer's three interchangeable names for the Greeks — the invading army besieging Troy. Homer also calls them Argives and Danaans; there is no difference in meaning.
The defenders of the city of Troy and its surrounding people, led by Hector under King Priam — together with allied contingents from across Asia Minor.
Achilles' own fierce contingent of warriors from Phthia. When he withdraws, they withdraw with him, and the Greeks feel the gap.
A people of Asia Minor, allied to Troy, led by Sarpedon and Glaucus — among the strongest of the Trojan allies.
The great walled city under siege, near the coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) — also called Ilium. The whole poem unfolds on the plain before its walls.
The high mountain that is home of the gods, above the world of mortals, where Zeus holds court and the gods argue over the war.
The mountain range above Troy from which Zeus often watches the fighting and directs the course of the war.
The chief river of the plain of Troy — also called Xanthus. Its banks see some of the fiercest fighting.
A major Greek city and kingdom; 'Argos' and 'Argives' are also used loosely for Greece and the Greeks as a whole.
Agamemnon's rich and powerful kingdom in the Greek mainland — the seat of the leader of the whole expedition.
Menelaus' kingdom in Greece, and Helen's home before Paris carried her to Troy.
Achilles' homeland in Greece, ruled by his father Peleus — the home he longs for and threatens to sail back to.
Odysseus' island kingdom, far to the west — the home he is famous for striving to return to.
The narrow strait (today the Dardanelles) beside which the Greek ships are beached — the army's lifeline and line of retreat.
Nestor's prosperous kingdom on the Greek coast.
The large island kingdom ruled by Idomeneus, which sent a strong contingent to the war.
The poem's first word and true subject — the wrath of Achilles (Greek mēnis). Not ordinary anger but a towering, ruinous fury that he nurses against his own side, with deadly consequences.
Greek timē — a warrior's public worth, measured in respect and in tangible prizes. To strip a man of his prize is to strip his honor, and that insult, not greed, is what ignites the quarrel.
Greek kleos — the undying fame a hero wins by great deeds, the 'glory that does not die.' Since a warrior's life is short, kleos is the nearest thing to immortality he can earn.
Greek geras — the share of war-spoils (treasure, armor, or a captive) awarded to a warrior as a public token of his honor. Briseis is Achilles' geras; taking her is a calculated insult.

Greek xenia — the sacred bond of hospitality between host and guest, protected by Zeus himself. Paris violated it by stealing Helen from his host Menelaus; it also lets enemies on the field recognize an old family tie and refuse to fight.
A hero's day of supreme excellence — a sustained battlefield rampage in which a single warrior dominates, like Diomedes' great day. The Greek word means 'being the best.'
The portion of life and death allotted to each person (Greek moira / aisa) — a destiny that even Zeus is reluctant to overrule. Heroes know their span is fixed and choose how to spend it.
A grand sacrifice to the gods — strictly a hundred oxen, but used for any large ritual offering meant to win divine favor or lift a curse.
A ritual pouring of wine onto the ground or altar as an offering to the gods, usually before a prayer, oath, or meal.
Treasure offered to buy back a captive or a body. The poem opens with a refused ransom (for Chryseis) and closes with an accepted one (for Hector's body).
The ghost or soul of a dead person, which goes down to the house of Hades — a faint, strengthless image of the living self.
Athletic contests — chariot racing, boxing, wrestling, footraces — held to honor a dead hero, with rich prizes awarded by the mourner.
The terrifying storm-shield (or goatskin mantle) of Zeus, often wielded by Athena or Apollo — when shaken over a battlefield it spreads panic or courage like a weapon.
Bronze shin-guards strapped over the lower legs — part of a warrior's armor, so standard that the Greeks are called 'well-greaved.'
The clear, immortal fluid that runs in the gods' veins in place of blood — when a god is wounded on the field, ichor flows.
The food of the gods, which (with nectar, their drink) sustains their immortality and is sometimes used to preserve a hero's body.
A stringed instrument plucked to accompany song and poetry — the very instrument a bard would use to sing a tale like the Iliad.
The great stack of wood on which a dead body is burned in funeral rites, the ashes then gathered for burial.
The Greek fleet, beached in a long line on the shore by Troy — the army's home, supply base, and only way back across the sea. Their hulls were sealed with dark pitch.
A light two-horse cart that carries a warrior swiftly to and across the battlefield, driven by a charioteer so the fighter can dismount to duel.
Father of Agamemnon and Menelaus; the two are constantly called 'the sons of Atreus.'
Achilles's father, a mortal married to the sea-goddess Thetis; Achilles is often named 'son of Peleus.'
Agamemnon's wife back home, whom he says he values less than the captive Chryseis.
Father of Zeus; Zeus is repeatedly called 'son of Cronus.'
The high mountain that is home of the gods.
The island where Hephaestus landed when Zeus once hurled him from heaven.
A hymn of praise and thanksgiving, here sung to Apollo to appease him.
A staff carried as the emblem of a king's or speaker's authority; whoever holds it has the floor.
A standing title for Apollo, the archer-god who strikes from a distance with his arrows.
A recurring epithet of Achilles, marking him as the fastest of the Greek runners.
A standing epithet for Hera, queen of the gods and wife of Zeus.
Zeus's and Athena's terrifying divine shield (the aegis), tasseled with gold, that spreads panic in battle.
Agamemnon's chief herald and messenger.
A herald serving Agamemnon (and elsewhere Odysseus).
A distant, blameless people at the edge of the world, where Zeus and the gods go to feast.
The great river the ancients believed encircled the whole earth.
A region of Asia Minor, allied with or neighboring Troy.
An ancestor of Agamemnon, in the descent of the royal scepter.
Brother of Atreus and a holder of the family scepter before Agamemnon.
Another name for the city of Troy.
A stretch of the Aegean, used in a simile for a heaving, storm-tossed crowd.
The Greek harbor where the fleet first gathered before sailing to Troy, site of the serpent omen.
A sign sent by the gods that foretells the future, such as the serpent that ate the sparrow's chicks.
The ugliest, most foul-mouthed common soldier, who rails at Agamemnon until Odysseus beats him into silence.
Odysseus's son back home; Odysseus swears 'by the father of Telemachus.'
Father of Diomedes, a famous warrior of the earlier generation against Thebes.
Diomedes's charioteer and close comrade, son of Capaneus.
Leader of the Athenian contingent, peerless at marshaling troops.
A Greek people from the region of Boeotia, listed first in the Catalogue of Ships.
A Greek people from Phocis in the army's muster.
A Greek people led by the lesser Ajax, son of Oileus.
Fierce long-haired warriors from Euboea in the Greek host.
Legendary earth-born founder-king of Athens, raised by Athena.
The region of Sparta, Menelaus's and Helen's homeland.
Son of Heracles, leader of the Rhodians, later killed in his duel with Sarpedon.
The great hero of the earlier age, ancestor of several leaders, who once sacked Troy himself.
The first Greek killed at Troy, struck down as he leapt from his ship; his men still mourn him.
A master archer left behind on Lemnos, suffering from a festering snakebite.
The great healer; his sons Machaon and Podalirius serve as the army's physicians.
A Thracian bard who boasted he could outsing the Muses and was crippled by them in punishment.
Goddesses of song and memory, daughters of Zeus, invoked by the poet to recall the Catalogue of Ships.
Goddess of grain and the harvest; her name stands for grain itself in similes of winnowing.
The second river of the Trojan plain, often paired with the Scamander.
A monstrous figure said to lie pinned beneath the earth, which groans when Zeus lashes the ground over him.
The dread underworld river by which the gods swear their most binding oaths.
A son of Priam, a Trojan lookout whose shape Iris borrows.
A Trojan people led by Aeneas, kin to the Trojans.
A Trojan nobleman, mortal father of Aeneas by Aphrodite.
The mountain near Troy, haunt of the gods and the spring of its rivers.
Pandarus's home town at the foot of Mount Ida.
A warlike northern people allied with Troy, known for wearing their hair in a topknot.
A people from the south Black Sea coast fighting for Troy.
An old people of the region, here counted among Troy's spear-fighting allies.
A legendary race of warrior women 'who fight like men.'
Paris's other name; the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen began the war.
The main western gates of Troy, where the elders sit and Hector meets his family.
The loveliest of Priam's daughters.
Helen's brother, a horse-tamer; one of the twin Dioscuri.
Helen's brother, a famous boxer; twin of Castor (the Roman Pollux).
The island where Paris first lay with Helen after carrying her off.
The body armor protecting the chest, also called a corselet or cuirass.
A piece of body armor covering the torso, often worked from bronze or layered linen.
The plume of horsehair nodding atop a warrior's helmet, meant to look fearsome.
The goddess of youth who pours nectar for the gods and tends the wounded Ares.
A town sacred to Athena, who is sometimes called 'Athena of Alalcomenae.'
The gray-eyed warrior-goddess of wisdom and battle, fierce champion of the Greeks.
A son of Antenor whose likeness Athena takes to find Pandarus.
Agamemnon's charioteer.
A Cretan captain, comrade of Idomeneus, deadly in battle.
An Argive leader of the earlier war against Thebes, companion of Tydeus.
The seven-gated city in Greece besieged a generation earlier by Tydeus and the Seven.
The people of Thebes, descendants of Cadmus.
Father of Sthenelus, one of the heroes of the older Theban war.
The personified spirit of discord, sister of Ares, who 'rears up small at first, then plants her head in the sky.'
The personified spirit of panic-flight that drives men from battle.
A young Trojan, named for the river Simois, killed by Telamonian Ajax.
The high citadel of Troy, where Apollo's temple stands.
A Greek people from Elis; their captain falls beside the Thracian leader.
A goddess of war and slaughter, 'sacker of cities,' companion to Ares.
Goddesses of beauty and charm who wove Aphrodite's divine robe.
A goddess, mother of Aphrodite, who comforts and heals her wounded daughter on Olympus.
One of the giant sons of Aloeus who once imprisoned the god Ares in a bronze jar.
The physician of the gods, who heals the wounded Ares and Hades.
Diomedes's wife, whom Dione warns will mourn him.
An early king of Troy whose godlike horses Aeneas's line secretly bred from.
A former king of Troy, famous for cheating the gods and heroes of their due.
The hip-socket joint, where Diomedes's hurled stone shatters Aeneas's hip.
A son of Priam, the best of the Trojan seers, who sends Hector into the city.
Wife of Antenor and priestess of Athena in Troy, who offers the robe to the goddess.
A wealthy Phoenician city whose women wove the robes Paris brought to Troy.
A bond of hospitality (xenia) passed down between families, so strong that Glaucus and Diomedes refuse to fight.
An ancestral hero of Glaucus who slew the Chimaera and survived deadly trials in Lycia.
A fire-breathing monster, part lion, part goat, part serpent, killed by Bellerophon.
The most cunning of men, an ancestor of Glaucus's line.
A king of Argos who, deceived by his wife, plotted Bellerophon's death.
Wife of Proetus, who falsely accused Bellerophon after he refused her.
A fierce people Bellerophon fought as one of his trials.
The god of wine, here recalled as a child driven into the sea by the impious Lycurgus.
A king who attacked the god Dionysus and was struck blind and short-lived in punishment.
Andromache's father, king of Thebe under Mount Placus, killed by Achilles.
A city under Mount Placus, home of Andromache, sacked by Achilles (distinct from Greek Thebes).
Andromache's people, ruled by her father Eetion.
A staff that holds wool or flax for spinning; with the loom it stands for women's domestic work.
A Greek captain, son of Mecisteus, who kills several Trojans in Book 6.
A Trojan who begs Menelaus for his life but is killed when Agamemnon intervenes.
A generous, hospitable Trojan from Arisbe, killed by Diomedes despite his kindness to strangers.
A Trojan-allied town, home of Axylus and Asius.
A standing Homeric phrase for the deep sea, dark like wine.
A standing epithet for Dawn, the goddess of morning who brings the daylight.
A formulaic epithet for a king or commander as protector of his men.
A formula marking a warrior as a fierce, war-bred fighter, as if descended from the war-god.
A burial mound heaped over a hero's body and ashes.
The upright frame on which women wove cloth; Helen weaves the war's battles into a tapestry.
The drink of the gods, served at their feasts; with ambrosia it sustains their immortality.
Marked tokens shaken in a helmet to decide by chance, here who throws first in the duel.
A legendary race of tiny men said to war with the cranes each year.
An ancient unit of length (roughly a forearm); Hector's spear is eleven cubits long.
A small unit of length, the width of a hand; Pandarus's bow-horns ran sixteen palms.
A Trojan herald, a wise man who stops the duel of Hector and Ajax and later carries Priam's peace offer to the Greeks.
The master leather-worker of Hyle who made Ajax's famous sevenfold ox-hide shield.
A warrior of old called the Mace-man because he fought with an iron club rather than bow or spear. Killed by Lycurgus.
A champion of old who wore the armor of King Areithous and challenged the best of the Greeks; young Nestor killed him.
A Greek captain, son of Euaemon, among the warriors who volunteer to face Hector. Later wounded in the thigh by an arrow from Paris.
A Greek leader, son of Andraemon, one of the nine who rise to face Hector in single combat.
Son of Jason and Hypsipyle, who sent ships of wine from Lemnos to the Greek camp.
Queen of Lemnos who bore Euneus to Jason.
The island home of Ajax, son of Telamon.
A rushing river by which the men of Pylos and the Arcadians once fought in Nestor's youth.
A town near which Nestor fought as a young man.
The town where Menesthius, an early victim of Paris, had lived.
The deepest pit beneath the earth, as far below Hades as the sky is above the ground, where Zeus threatens to fling any disobedient god.
A peak of Mount Ida where Zeus keeps a sacred grove and altar and sits to watch the war.
The dark underworld region of the dead, out of which a Fury hears Althaea's curse and from which Heracles fetched the hound of hell.
Hector's first charioteer, son of Thebaeus, killed by Diomedes' spear.
Hector's second charioteer, son of Iphitus, killed by an arrow from Teucer.
A brother of Hector who takes up the reins as his charioteer after Archeptolemus falls.
A son of Priam, struck in the chest by an arrow meant for Hector; his head droops like a poppy heavy with seed.
A bride from Aesyme, mother of Priam's son Gorgythion.
A loyal squire, son of Echius, who helps carry the wounded Teucer back to the ships.
The king who laid the famous labors on Heracles, including fetching the hound of hell from the underworld.
An ancient Titan who, with Cronus, sits imprisoned deep in Tartarus far from sun and wind.
Goddesses who keep the gates of heaven, rolling the cloud aside or closing it, and who tend the gods' horses.
A coastal town where the Greeks bring rich offerings to Poseidon.
A place sacred to Poseidon where the Greeks honor him with gifts.
A river of the Trojan plain (also called Scamander); also the name of one of Hector's horses.
The young son of Agamemnon, raised in luxury at home, named as a measure of honor for Achilles.
One of Agamemnon's three daughters, offered to Achilles in marriage.
One of Agamemnon's three daughters, offered to Achilles in marriage.
A wealthy Greek city whose riches Achilles names as something he still would not trade his honor for.
The sanctuary of Apollo at rocky Delphi, famed for the treasure stored behind its stone threshold.
Father of Phoenix, who cursed his son in a quarrel over a mistress.
The dread queen of the underworld, invoked in curses alongside Hades.
Avenging spirits of the dark who carry out curses, especially those of wronged parents.
The people of the borderlands of Phthia over whom Peleus set Phoenix as lord.
In Phoenix's parable, the lame daughters of Zeus who limp behind swift Ruin, healing the harm she does when men honor them.
In Phoenix's parable, the strong and swift force of blind folly that runs ahead and harms men, with Prayers following to mend it.
A hero of old whose anger kept him from defending Calydon; Phoenix tells his story as a warning to Achilles.
The city the hero Meleager defended, besieged by the Curetes while the Aetolians held it.
A people who warred against the Aetolians, fighting to bring down the city of Calydon.
The people who held and defended the city of Calydon against the Curetes.
King of Calydon and father of Meleager, who angered Artemis by neglecting her sacrifice.
Mother of Meleager, who cursed her own son in grief over her dead brother.
The wife of Meleager, who finally moved him to return to battle; also called Alcyone.
The strongest man of his day, who took up his bow against Apollo himself for the sake of Marpessa.
A beautiful woman carried off by Apollo and won back by Idas; mother of Cleopatra.
A woman of Lesbos, daughter of Phorbas, carried off by Achilles and shared his bed.
A woman given by Achilles to Patroclus, taken when he sacked Scyros.
The Greek homeland, used for Achilles' own country and the land of lovely women.
A Trojan herald, the father of the scout Dolon.
A Thracian king newly come to Troy, with horses whiter than snow and golden armor, killed by Diomedes in the night raid.
A famous thief who once stole the boar's-tusk helmet that Odysseus wears on the night raid.
An ancestral lord of Troy whose tomb or barrow stands in the middle of the plain.
A Thracian counselor, kinsman of Rhesus, woken by Apollo to discover the slaughter in the night raid.
A people allied to Troy, camped toward the sea.
A people allied to Troy, archers with curved bows.
A proud people counted among Troy's allies.
A people allied to Troy, masters of horses.
A people allied to Troy, masters of horses.
The mortal lover of Dawn, beside whose bed she rises each morning to bring light to gods and men.
A king of Cyprus who gave Agamemnon his ornate breastplate as a guest-gift.
A Trojan who, bribed by Paris, argued against returning Helen and urged killing the Greek envoys; father of Pisander and Hippolochus.
A brave son of Antenor, raised in Thrace, who wounds Agamemnon's belt and is killed by him.
Antenor's eldest son, who wounds Agamemnon in the arm avenging his brother Iphidamas, then is killed.
The goddesses of childbirth, daughters of Hera, who send sharp pangs on women in labor; the pain of Agamemnon's wound is likened to theirs.
A Greek healer, son of Asclepius and brother of Machaon, still fighting on the plain.
The wisest and most honest of the Centaurs, who taught Achilles the use of healing herbs.
A race of beings part man and part horse; Chiron, the most honest of them, was famed for his knowledge of medicine.
A Trojan, son of Hippasus, who wounds Odysseus in the side before Odysseus kills him.
The lovely captive woman, daughter of Arsinous, who mixes a restoring draught for Nestor in his hut.
A strong dark wine used in the restoring draught Hecamede mixes, blended with grated goat cheese and barley.
Twin sons of Actor (and truly of Poseidon), warriors Nestor recalls fighting in his youth, saved from him by their divine father.
A king of Elis who wrongfully kept Neleus's prize horses, recalled in Nestor's tale of his youth.
King of Pylos and father of Nestor; his many sons were killed by Heracles, leaving Nestor alone.
The people of Elis who warred against Nestor's Pylos in the cattle-raid of his youth.
A reckless Trojan ally, son of Hyrtacus, who refuses to leave his chariot and is killed assaulting the gates.
A strong Lapith captain, son of Pirithous, who holds the gates with Leonteus against Asius's charge.
A Lapith captain, equal to the war-god, who defends the gates beside Polypoetes.
A warlike Greek people; two of their champions, Polypoetes and Leonteus, defend the gate against the Trojan assault.
The herald Menestheus sends running to summon Ajax to the threatened wall.
A Greek who carries Teucer's bow as Ajax and Teucer go to defend the wall.
A comrade of Sarpedon, the first man Ajax kills at the wall, struck down by a great stone.
A warrior judged by Sarpedon among the best of the allies, set as a captain over the Lycian assault.
Father of Idomeneus, the Cretan king.
A formal duel of one champion against another, agreed between the armies, as when Hector challenges and Ajax meets him.
An epithet of Apollo, the archer god whose arrows strike from a distance.
An epithet of Poseidon, the god who shakes the earth and the sea.
A standard epic phrase for the deep open sea, dark like wine.
An old unit of length, roughly the forearm; Hector's spear is said to be eleven cubits long.
A gift exchanged between host and guest as a bond of friendship, as the helmet passed among many owners.
The gifts a suitor traditionally gave to win a wife; Agamemnon offers a daughter with no bride-price but a great dowry instead.
The payment a killer makes to the family of his victim to settle a death without further vengeance.
A wide belt worn in battle, sometimes given as a gift, as the purple belt Ajax gives Hector.
The backbone cut of a roasted animal, given as a portion of honor at the feast.
A three-legged bronze vessel or stand, a prized possession offered among gifts and won as a prize.
A large metal pot counted as treasure among the gifts Agamemnon offers Achilles.
The protective wall along the top of the rampart from which defenders fight.
The raised defensive wall of the Greek camp, stormed by the Trojans.
An island sacked by Achilles, from which came the seven skilled women offered to him.
A monstrous figure whose glaring head is shown on Agamemnon's shield and to which Hector's blazing eyes are compared.
A river of the underworld, across whose deep waters the dead pass; Heracles barely returned over it.
Father of Diomede, the woman of Lesbos taken by Achilles.
A steep city sacked by Achilles, from which he gave Iphis to Patroclus.
The home of Tychius, the leather-worker who made Ajax's shield.
The home from which Castianeira came as a bride to Priam.
A high island in the northern Aegean. Poseidon watches the battle from its wooded peak, where he can see all of Troy and the ships.
A small island off the coast near Troy. A great undersea cave lies between it and Imbros, where Poseidon stables his horses.
An island in the northern Aegean near Troy, named alongside Tenedos and Lemnos.
Divine, immortal, fit for the gods — used here of the fodder Poseidon sets before his immortal horses.
The pair of Greek warriors both named Ajax — the huge Ajax son of Telamon and the swift Ajax son of Oileus — who often fight side by side.
The 'lesser' or swift Ajax, leader of the Locrians, fast on his feet and deadly in pursuit. Distinct from the larger Ajax son of Telamon.
The huge, towering Greek warrior, second only to Achilles in battle. He defends the ships with a great shield 'like a tower.'
A son of Priam and brother of Hector, a bold Trojan fighter. He is wounded in the hand by Meriones.
A Trojan spearman, son-in-law of Priam, killed by Teucer in Book XIII.
A Greek warrior, grandson of Actor, killed by Hector's spear as he enters the fighting.
A Trojan ally who sought to marry Priam's daughter Cassandra by promising to drive off the Greeks. Idomeneus kills him.
The loveliest of Priam's daughters, sought in marriage by Othryoneus.
A Trojan, son-in-law of Anchises, struck down by Idomeneus while Poseidon holds him frozen in place.
A noble Trojan leader who helps wounded comrades and fights in the front ranks.
A Trojan who fights Menelaus with an axe and is killed by him.
Son of the Paphlagonian king Pylaemenes, killed by an arrow from Meriones.
A rich Corinthian who sailed to Troy knowing he was fated to die there. Paris kills him with an arrow.
The terrible tasseled storm-shield of Zeus, fringed and dreadful, which routs men with panic. It is carried at times by Apollo and Athena.
A strap worn across the chest to carry a shield or sword. Hector's spear strikes where Ajax's two straps cross.
A piece of body armor protecting the chest, also called a breastplate or corslet.
A son of Nestor and brother of Antilochus, a Greek fighter held in reserve.
An ancient sea-goddess, wife of Ocean, who fostered Hera. Hera claims to be visiting her to mend the couple's quarrel.
The god of sleep, brother of Death. Hera bribes him to lull Zeus so she can deceive him.
Personified as a god, the twin brother of Sleep. With Sleep he carries Sarpedon's body home to Lycia.
One of the younger Graces, promised to Sleep in marriage as his reward.
The older gods, including Cronus, dwelling below the earth, called as witnesses to a god's most solemn oath.
The mortals' name for a shrill mountain bird (called chalcis by the gods); Sleep hides in a pine in its likeness.
The Titan mother of Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades by Cronus.
The narrow strait beside Troy (the modern Dardanelles) where the Greek ships are drawn up.
A Trojan, cousin of Hector, killed by Ajax as he tries to set fire to a ship.
A retainer of Ajax, honored like family, killed by Hector's spear.
A long jointed pole tipped with bronze, kept aboard ship for fighting at sea, which Ajax swings to defend the ships.
The father of Patroclus, an old hero living in Peleus's household.
One of Achilles' two immortal horses, paired with Xanthus.
A mortal trace-horse of Achilles, captured at Eetion's city, who keeps pace with the immortal pair until Sarpedon's spear kills him.
The wise centaur who cut the great Pelian ash spear and gave it to Peleus; only Achilles can wield it.
Achilles' great spear, made from an ash tree on Mount Pelion, so heavy that only he can lift it.
A captain of the Myrmidons, secret son of the god Hermes and Polymele.
The goddess of childbirth and its pains, who brings infants into the light.
An ancient oracle of Zeus in a wintry land, served by the Selloi. Achilles prays to 'Zeus of Dodona.'
The barefoot priests of Zeus at Dodona who sleep on the ground and interpret his will.
Leader of the Paeonian horsemen and a Trojan ally, the first man Patroclus kills.
A monstrous fire-breathing creature, 'the ruin of many,' reared by Amisodarus, whose sons fight at Troy.
A panicked Trojan charioteer dragged from his car by Patroclus, compared to a fish hauled on a hook.
A young Trojan, son of Panthous, who is the first to wound Patroclus in the back. Menelaus later kills him.
A Trojan ally, son of Lethus the Pelasgian, killed by Ajax while dragging off Patroclus's body.
The home city of the Pelasgian allies of Troy, far from which Hippothous dies.
The best of the Phocians, a Greek leader killed by Hector's spear.
A Trojan ally, son of Phaenops, killed by Ajax over the body of Hippothous.
A Greek warrior who avenges his comrade Leiocritus by killing Apisaon.
A warrior's attendant and second-in-command in battle; Patroclus is repeatedly called Achilles' squire.
The charioteer of Meriones, killed by Hector but in dying saves Idomeneus's life.
A rich Trojan and dear feast-companion of Hector, killed by Menelaus.
The old sea-god, father of Thetis and the Nereids, dwelling in the depths of the sea.
The sea-nymph daughters of Nereus who gather to mourn with Thetis when Achilles cries out in grief.
One of the famous Nereids, sea-nymph daughters of Nereus named in Thetis's gathering.
An Aegean island to which Hera's storm drove Heracles after he sacked Troy.
A daughter of Ocean who, with Thetis, sheltered the lame Hephaestus for nine years after his fall from heaven.
The 'bright-headdressed' wife of Hephaestus, who welcomes Thetis into the smith-god's house.
A cluster of stars Hephaestus sets on the shield of Achilles among the constellations.
A group of stars worked onto the shield of Achilles.
A great constellation depicted on the shield of Achilles, watched by the Bear.
The constellation also called the Wagon, which wheels in place and never sinks below the horizon, shown on Achilles' shield.
The great five-layered shield Hephaestus forges, its face worked with the earth, sky, sea, two cities, fields, herds, and a dancing-floor — a picture of the whole world.
Units of weight, here in gold, offered as a prize to the elder who judges most justly on the shield's city scene.
Official messengers and order-keepers who carry staves, hold back crowds, and serve at feasts and judgments.
The senior men who sit in a sacred circle to give judgment in the city scene on the shield.
A traditional mourning or harvest song sung by a boy with a lyre in the vineyard scene on the shield.
The legendary craftsman who built a famous dancing-floor for Ariadne at Cnossus, the model for the one on the shield.
A princess of Crete for whom Daedalus made his famous dancing-floor at Cnossus.
The great city of Crete where Daedalus built Ariadne's dancing-floor.
The wind-god sire of Achilles' immortal horses, fathered on the storm-mare Podarge.
The storm-mare who bore Achilles' immortal horses Xanthus and Balius to the West Wind.
The wife of Oileus and stepmother of the bastard Medon, whose kinsman Medon killed, forcing him to flee.
A bastard son of Oileus and brother of Ajax, living in exile at Phylace; a Greek leader killed by Aeneas.
A people allied with Troy; Apollo takes the shape of their lord Mentes to rouse Hector.
A broad shovel used to toss grain into the wind so the chaff blows away; an arrow glances off Menelaus's armor like beans leaping from it.
A water-nymph; one bore the Trojan Satnius to Enops by the river Satnioeis.
A town near Troy that Achilles sacked; Briseis was taken there.
The goddess of ruinous blindness, eldest daughter of Zeus. She is the delusion that leads men to disaster; Zeus once hurled her from heaven.
An avenging spirit of the underworld that punishes oaths broken and blood spilled. The Furies stop the speaking horse and witness Agamemnon's oath.
aliases: the Fury who walks in the dark

glossary.gloss: The mortal mother of Heracles. Hera delayed her labor to cheat Zeus of his oath.
A famous hero of an older generation, grandfather of Eurystheus.
A unit of weight, here of gold; part of the gifts and ransom. Ten talents of gold are weighed out for Achilles.
The young son of Achilles, raised on Scyros.
A king whose city Achilles sacked; Briseis' first husband was among the slain there.
A name for the sun, whose blazing brightness Achilles' armor is likened to.
The mountain whose ash-wood furnished Achilles' great spear.
A companion of Achilles who helps yoke the horses and waits on him.
The goddess of right order, sent by Zeus to summon the gods to assembly.
A hill near Troy where the pro-Trojan gods take their seat to watch the battle.
A son of Priam; both the Trojan whose shape Apollo borrows, and the young prince Achilles spares once but kills at the river.
A people allied to Troy, ruled by Altes.
The ancestor of the Trojan royal line, a son of Zeus who founded Dardania.
The early settlement on the slopes of Ida, founded by Dardanus before Troy itself was built.
An early Trojan king, richest of men, whose mares were loved by the North Wind.
The North Wind, here a stallion-shaped god who sires foals; later summoned to fan Patroclus' pyre.
The most beautiful of mortals, caught up by the gods to pour Zeus's wine and live among the immortals.
A son of Tros, ancestor of Aeneas through Capys and Anchises.
A Trojan ancestor, son of Assaracus and father of Anchises.
A people allied with Troy, at whose position Poseidon sets Aeneas down out of danger.
A walled mound on the plain, raised long ago so Heracles could flee a sea-monster; the Greek-friendly gods sit there.
A Trojan captain, son of Otrynteus, the first man Achilles kills in his renewed rampage.
The father of Iphition, a sacker of cities from the land of Hyde.
A snowy mountain in Lydia near Iphition's homeland.
A brave Trojan, son of Antenor, killed by a spear through the helmet and temple.
A Trojan Achilles spears in the back as he flees his chariot, dying with a bull-like bellow.
The youngest and dearest son of Priam, swift of foot; Achilles kills him as he shows off his speed.
A Trojan killed by Achilles with a spear through the neck.
A big, strong Trojan, son of Philetor, downed at the knee and finished with the sword.
One of two sons of Bias thrown from their chariot and killed by Achilles.
A young Trojan who clasps Achilles' knees begging for mercy and is killed anyway.
A Trojan Achilles spears through the ear.
A Trojan, son of Agenor, split open by Achilles' sword.
A brave warrior from Thrace, speared in the belly by Achilles.
A rich land north of Troy that sent allies to the Trojans.
A river-god of Paeonia, ancestor of Asteropaeus.
A distant land whose people, the Paeonians, came to fight for Troy under Asteropaeus.
A famous warrior, son of the river Axius and father of Asteropaeus.
A great river, named as lesser than Zeus when Achilles boasts of his divine descent.
A son of Zeus, father of Peleus and grandfather of Achilles.
One who begs protection or mercy, clasping the knees of the powerful; custom and the gods demand they be respected.
A wife of Priam, daughter of Altes, mother of Lycaon and Polydorus.
The aged king of the Lelegians, father of Laothoe and grandfather of Lycaon.
The star Sirius, brightest in the sky, a sign of evil bringing fever; Achilles' armor blazes like it.
A title of Athena used by Zeus as he humors her wish to let Achilles kill Hector.
A gate of Troy that Hector keeps trying to reach as Achilles chases him around the walls.
The evening star, loveliest in the sky; Achilles' spear-point gleams like it as he kills Hector.
A wooded mountain above Thebe, Andromache's homeland.
The frame or couch on which a body is laid out for mourning and carried to the pyre.
A river-god of Achilles' homeland to whom Peleus had vowed to cut Achilles' hair; Achilles gives the lock to Patroclus instead.
The West Wind, summoned with Boreas to make Patroclus' pyre blaze.
The star that heralds the dawn; it rises as Patroclus' pyre at last burns down.
The first and grandest contest of Patroclus' funeral games, run around a distant turning-post.
The mark far out on the plain that the racing chariots must round; skill at hugging it wins the race.
Son of Admetus and the finest horseman in the race, who is wrecked when Athena breaks his yoke and finishes last.
The father of Eumelus, the skilled charioteer.
Agamemnon's swift mare, lent to Menelaus for the chariot race.
Menelaus' own horse, yoked beside Agamemnon's mare in the race.
The swift, half-divine horse of Adrestus, named by Nestor as the fastest of all.
The swift but lesser Ajax, who quarrels with Idomeneus and is tripped by Athena in the footrace.
The great, massive Ajax; he wrestles Odysseus to a draw and competes in several games.
The father of the great Ajax.
The father of Odysseus, who is often called 'son of Laertes.'
A big, boastful Greek and the best boxer in the games; he knocks out Euryalus with one blow.
The father of the boxer Epeius.
A king of Thebes at whose funeral games Mecisteus once triumphed.
The founder of Thebes; the Thebans are called 'sons of Cadmus.'
An unworked lump of iron, once thrown by Eetion, set as a prize for the weight-throwing contest.
Of Phoenicia, the seafaring traders who carried the silver bowl across the sea.
A lord at whose funeral games at Buprasium the young Nestor won many contests.
A place in Elis where Nestor recalls winning the funeral games of Amarynceus.
A mother whose twelve children Apollo and Artemis killed for her boast against Leto; even she, turned to stone, remembered to eat. Achilles tells her tale to coax Priam to supper.
The lonely mountain where Niobe, turned to stone, broods over her grief.
A son of Priam named among those rebuked by their father.
A son of Priam, named in his father's angry rebuke.
A son of Priam, godlike, whom Priam mourns as lost.
A son of Priam who fought from his chariot, mourned by his father as dead.
An island near Troy named among the places captives were sold and a marker of the sea Iris dives through.
The supposed father Hermes claims when he meets Priam in the guise of a young Myrmidon.
A formal mourning-song led over the dead; singers chant it over Hector while the women wail in answer.
The earthen barrow heaped over a grave to honor and mark the dead; mounds are raised for Patroclus and Hector.
To gorge or satisfy to the full, especially of bloodshed: to glut Ares with blood means to give war its fill of killing.
A shallow crossing-place of a river; the Trojans flee to the ford of the Xanthus.
